13-124.r: Free trade policy → goods and services cross borders with little or no tariffs, quotas, subsidies or bans; i.e. absence of tariff.

13-125.r: Free Trade Zones (SEZs/FTWZs) → set up to promote export industries; goods landed, made and re-exported generally free of customs duty.

13-127.r: Special Economic Zone (SEZ) policy in India → announced 1 April 2000, to boost foreign investment and give a hassle-free environment for exports.

13-129.r: SEZ Act 2005 → passed May 2005, assent 23 June 2005, in force 10 February 2006; aims: economic activity, exports of goods and services, investment, jobs, infrastructure.
13-129.t: Passed in 2005 but effective in 2006; it promotes exports of goods and services, not services only.

13-134.r: Asia's first EPZ → Kandla (Gujarat), 1965; Chennai, Kandla, Kochi and Surat all have SEZs (converted EPZs), so no option fits.

13-137.r: Free Trade Zones: Kandla, Mumbai, Visakhapatnam had them; Thiruvananthapuram had none in the question period (now has SEZs, notified 2006).

13-138.r: India's first EPZ → 1965; SEZ policy → 2000; Vadodara → Patola silk (as per book); Panna (MP) → diamond mining, not gold mines.
13-138.c: Patola silk is usually linked with Patan (Gujarat); the book accepts Vadodara as correct.

13-139.r: First private-sector EPZ → Surat (1997), converted into SEZ from 1 November 2000; run by Diamond and Gem Development Corporation (DGDC).

13-140.r: Nandigram (Purba Medinipur, West Bengal) → Salim Group allowed a chemical hub under SEZ policy in 2007; villagers protested heavily.

13-141.r: SEZ export growth among 2004-05 to 2007-08 → highest in 2007-08 (93%); later peak 121.40% in 2009-10.

13-142.r: Most approved and operational SEZs (June 2012) → Andhra Pradesh; now Tamil Nadu has most operational, Telangana most approved (276 operational SEZs, 31.12.2023).

13-143.r: SEZ India mobile app → launched January 2017 by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (e-Governance initiative).

13-144.r: Channelising India's exports and imports → MMTC, Exim Bank, State Trading Corporation and Food Corporation of India: all four.

13-145.r: EXIM Bank of India → set up in 1982 under the Export-Import Bank of India Act, 1981; purveyor of export credit.
13-145.t: Don't confuse the Act year (1981) with the year the bank was set up (1982).

13-146.r: Foreign trade promotion bodies → ECGC (export credit risk insurance), STC and MMTC: all of the above.

13-147.r: ECGC (Export Credit Guarantee Corporation, set up 1957, Government of India) → export financing and credit risk insurance for exporters.

13-151.r: EPCG → Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme: import of capital goods without customs duty to make quality export goods.

13-152.r: NIRVIK (Niryat Rin Vikas Yojana), Budget 2020-21 → export sector: higher insurance cover and lower premium for small exporters.

13-153.r: India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF) → Trust set up in 1996 by the Department of Commerce to promote the 'Made in India' label abroad.

13-154.r: Morgan Stanley (1998) → India 3rd among emerging markets, after Brazil (1st) and Mexico (2nd).

13-155.r: India's tourism industry is small for its size and potential because tourist infrastructure is inadequate.

13-156.r: Most visited country (World Tourism Organization 2006, and in 2022) → France; in 2022 followed by Spain and USA.

13-157.r: UNWTO Report 2010 → France was the most visited country in the world (still top in 2022).

13-158.r: Most favoured destination of Indian tourists in 2010 → Singapore; in 2022 → UAE (28.0%), then Saudi Arabia, USA, Singapore, UK.

13-159.r: Foreign Tourist Arrivals fell in 2009 (–2.2%, to 5.17 million from 5.28 million in 2008) → answer 2009-10.

13-160.r: Top State in foreign tourist visits (question period) → Maharashtra; in 2022 → Gujarat first (20.70%), Maharashtra second.

13-161.r: Top State in domestic tourist visits (question period) → Andhra Pradesh; in 2022 → Uttar Pradesh (317.91 million), Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh.

13-162.r: Travel + Leisure survey 2009 → Udaipur best city in the world for tourism; in 2023 Udaipur was 2nd after Oaxaca (Mexico).

13-163.r: Nathu La (Sikkim–Tibet pass) → reopened in 2006 for India-China border trade; sealed for about 4 decades after 1959.

13-164.r: India-Australia ECTA (Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement) → signed 2 April 2022, in force from 29 December 2022.

13-165.r: 16 February 2011 → India signed a Free Trade Agreement (CEPA) with Japan.
13-165.t: Don't mix: Japan (CEPA) and Malaysia (CECA) agreements were both signed in February 2011.

13-166.r: 18 February 2011 → India signed a Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement with Malaysia at Putrajaya.

13-167.r: Israel–UAE Free Trade Agreement → signed 31 May 2022; Israel's first FTA with an Arab country (aim: trade above US$ 10 billion).

13-168.r: January 2002 → China and Bangladesh signed a bilateral Free Trade Agreement.

13-169.r: Most anti-dumping measures in 1995-2005 → India (WTO data); in 2022 the USA had the most measures in effect (493).

13-170.r: 'Super 301' (Special 301) → US Trade Representative's annual process naming foreign trade barriers to US exports, i.e. blockade in free trade.

13-171.r: IITF 2021 (40th edition, ITPO) → theme 'Atmanirbhar Bharat', held November 2021 at Pragati Maidan, New Delhi, not Jaipur.

13-172.r: Import quota → physical control (limits quantity of imports to protect domestic producers); the correctly matched pair.

13-173.r: Open general licence → External trade; TRYSEM → Employment; Wholesale Price Index → Inflation; Cash Reserve Ratio → Debt control.

14-001.r: Full rupee convertibility advocated to attract more foreign capital; LERMS from March 1992; rupee fully convertible on current account in August 1994 (IMF Article VIII).

14-008.r: Liberalized Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) → announced in Union Budget 1992-93; partial convertibility with dual rate (market interbank rate + RBI official rate).

14-009.r: Full convertibility of rupee → free float with other currencies and direct exchange anywhere inside or outside India; it does not make rupee an international currency.

14-010.r: Rupee is fully convertible only on current account (since August 1994); capital account convertibility is partial; not convertible into gold.

14-012.r: Capital account → foreign loans, FDI, portfolio investment; private remittances belong to the current account.

14-013.r: S.S. Tarapore Committees (RBI) → capital account convertibility: first report May 1997; second on fuller CAC, report 31 July 2006.

14-015.r: Devaluation → official lowering of a currency's value against major international currencies (fixed exchange rate); rupee devalued in 1949, 1966 and 1991.
14-015.t: Devalued in three years but four times: 1991 had two steps (July 1 and July 3).

14-018.r: July 1991 rupee devaluation → about 18% in two steps (1 and 3 July); 17.38% against pound sterling, about 18.7% in US dollar terms; financial year 1991-92.

14-020.r: Devaluation necessarily makes exports more competitive only; it lowers the currency's foreign value and need not improve trade balance (costly essential imports like crude).

14-021.r: Devaluation → country's goods become cheaper abroad, so exports rise and imports become costly: A and R true, R explains A.

14-026.r: Devaluation does not cause deflation in the importing country; it raises the prices of imported goods and the domestic price level.

14-027.r: India's export growth rose after 1991 because of devaluation (about 18% on 1 and 3 July 1991) and export promotion: A and R true, R explains A.

14-028.r: International liquidity problem → shortage of dollars and other hard currencies (resources to finance BoP deficits: gold, SDRs, foreign currencies).

14-029.r: Late-1990s East Asian crisis (Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, South Korea) → prolonged over-valuation of local currencies; began in Thailand, July 1997.

14-030.r: South-East Asian currency devaluations (1997-98) → unfavourable for Indian exports, which compete with theirs.

14-031.r: Immunity from a global financial crisis → avoid short-term foreign borrowings; more foreign banks and full capital account convertibility would increase risk.

14-032.r: Reduce currency crisis risk → IT sector forex earnings and remittances from Indians abroad; more government expenditure does not help.

14-033.r: To stop rupee slide: curb non-essential imports, promote exports, Masala Bonds, easier ECB rules; not expansionary monetary policy (it raises rupee supply).

14-034.r: Higher duties on exports cut exports, so they do not help BoP; import substitution, devaluation and higher import tariffs can help.

14-035.r: Reduce current account deficit → devalue currency and attract FDI/FII funds; cutting export subsidy would reduce exports, so it does not help.

14-036.r: Highest FDI inflows: Telecommunication in the question period (per explanation); Services sector leads April 2000 to March 2024 (16.13%).
14-036.c: Printed answer (b) Services uses current data; the explanation says (d) Telecommunication was correct for the question period.

14-037.r: Sector attracting the highest FDI equity inflow in India → Service sector.
